analysis.one_liner: Requires members of Congress to divest or blind-trust their individual stocks and similar investments.
analysis.headline: Nine Senate Democrats backed the ban, but the bill was referred to committee on September 12, 2023, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every member of Congress to sell off or place in a blind trust any individually held stocks, commodities, futures, or similar investments — including those held by a spouse or a dependent child under 19 — for their entire time in office plus 180 days after leaving. It exempts diversified mutual funds, exchange-traded funds, and Treasury bonds, so members could keep broad, diversified investments. Members who failed to comply would face a fine equal to one month of their congressional salary, charged again every 30 days until they complied.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens would benefit from reduced conflicts of interest: lawmakers voting on bills and overseeing industries could no longer personally profit from moves in individual company stocks, commodities, or futures. Members of Congress and their families would also be protected from accusations of trading on inside knowledge of legislation.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each member of Congress, their spouse, and any dependent child under 19 to divest or place in an ethics-office-approved blind trust every individually held security, commodity, future, or derivative — including holdings through investment funds, trusts, and deferred-compensation plans
The ban applies for a member's entire time in Congress and for 180 days after leaving office, preventing last-minute trades on the way out the door
Members who do not comply face a civil fine equal to one month of their congressional salary, assessed 30 days after notice and repeated at least every 30 days until they comply
All certifications, blind-trust agreements, asset schedules, extensions, and penalties must be posted publicly on ethics-office websites, so compliance is visible to voters
Members may keep diversified mutual funds, diversified ETFs, and Treasury bonds, and may not acquire new individual stock-type investments while serving

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress who hold individual stocks, commodities, futures, or derivatives would have to sell them or give up control through a blind trust, and their spouses and young children would face the same requirement. Ethically it costs officeholders money and control; the public cost is minimal, limited to administering the system through the ethics offices.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement is a civil fine equal to one month's salary, assessed and collected by the same congressional ethics offices that regulate members — there is no criminal penalty, so for a wealthy member the recurring fine could function as a fee for continuing to trade
The ban covers dependent children under 19 but not adult children or other relatives, leaving a legal path for a member's investments to be held by grown children outside the blind-trust requirement

Members would have 120 days to divest or blind-trust holdings, with up to 180 days of extensions, so a sudden compliance deadline could force large sell-offs, though extensions are designed to soften this

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core rules are practical: diversified mutual funds and Treasuries remain allowed, and blind trusts are an established mechanism, so compliance is achievable rather than punishing. The design's real weaknesses are in enforcement — a fine set by an office controlled by Congress itself, capped at one month's pay per month, with adult children simply excluded. The bill would have closed the most visible conflict of interest (a member's own portfolio) but would not have eliminated every route for a congressional household's money to stay tied to companies awaiting legislative action.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Ossoff introduced the bill on September 12, 2023, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors: Kelly, Warnock, Bennet, Duckworth, Luján, Schatz, Baldwin, and Shaheen

The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs — and the action history shows no markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor action ever followed
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired in committee without ever receiving a vote in the Senate or the House

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress who hold individual stocks are better off: they keep the ability to buy and trade securities connected to sectors they legislate on, subject only to the existing disclosure rules rather than divestiture or a blind trust.

for.name: Sen. Jon Ossoff
for.role: U.S. Senator from Georgia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ban Congressional Stock Trading Act, requiring divestiture or blind trusts for members' individual stock holdings

for.name: Eight Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors: Kelly, Warnock, Bennet, Duckworth, Luján, Schatz, Baldwin, and Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the ban

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Sen. Gary Peters, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 12, 2023 and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or committee vote on it; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought any congressional stock-trading ban to the Senate floor for a vote during the 118th Congress, despite multiple versions pending

sides.party_line_note: All nine Senate sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never reached a roll-call vote in either chamber, so the partisan split is visible only in sponsorship.

industries.industry: Members of Congress who hold individual securities
industries.note: The bill directly restricts the officeholders themselves: they and their spouses and young dependents would have to sell or blind-trust individual stocks, commodities, futures, and derivatives, facing a repeating one-month-salary fine for noncompliance. Their interest in keeping trading rights runs against the public's interest in lawmakers without personal financial stakes in the industries they regulate.

The bill would move some congressional households' money out of individually traded securities into diversified funds, Treasuries, and blind trusts — a modest outflow of a few hundred portfolios, not a market-wide effect. Brokerages and exchanges neither gain nor lose meaningfully.
